verdict.rationale: Both refactors look behaviour-preserving and similarly readable. Both use named states, small per-token-kind functions, and the error-to-stop logic in one place. A also pins the old behaviour with 18 new in-repo tests covering every error kind with exact positions, empty values, non-ASCII text and post-error iteration. B's equivalence checking lives only in an out-of-repo scratch crate, so nothing in the repository protects the refactor going forward.
a_issues: After an error, `pos` is no longer moved to the end of the line. This is invisible through the iterator but changes the internal state and `Debug` output, which the report discloses.
The `Scanned` struct adds a small extra abstraction layer.
b_issues: Adds no regression tests to the repo. The old-vs-new comparison sits in a scratch crate outside the repository, which is left behind next to the repo.
The report says the stop code was copied at nine error returns; the original actually has eleven.
`read_value` resets `expect` to `Token` even on error and relies on `next()` to override it to `Nothing`, which is a slightly indirect state flow.

verdict.rationale: Both refactors preserve behaviour: tracing every path (separator skipping, empty bare values, timestamp and quote scanning, quote-in-run errors, stop-after-error) gives the same tokens and error positions as the original, and neither should be slower. B also adds 18 regression tests that pin every error kind with its exact position, plus empty values, non-ASCII text and iteration after errors. Those tests protect the format work the developer is dreading, while A adds no tests. B's scanners take `&self` and return a `Scanned` result, so all state changes happen in `next()`, which is a slightly cleaner design than A's helpers mutating `self`.
